utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to one and all. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, we know the Prosecution, Defence. We have the witness here. And of course good morning to all the other people in the courtroom. As you know that today we are sitting in two sessions, the morning and in the afternoon as of 4.00 p.m., especially as the witness to be examined is arriving. But I've been told that the -- his plane is arriving at 7.00 p.m., which means we'll hear the witness tomorrow morning. Now, as far as the Defence is concerned, you have three hours left for the cross-examination. If you use those three hours prudently, we can finish this morning or around 1.00, 1.30, perhaps, and then we won't have to sit at 4.00 this afternoon, have an afternoon session. So we're going to have this morning's session certainly, and tomorrow's session, Wednesday, 9.00, with the next witness. And I'd like to remind you that tomorrow's witness - I have done the maths - the Defence has five hours and a quarter. So in theory, if you use your five hours, 15 minutes of cross-examination, we should be over with our work tomorrow with the second witness, which means automatically that we won't be having a session on Thursday morning because we will have run out of witnesses.(redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: (redacted)We're going to have a session not at 9.00 but at 2.15. So it will be the Tuesday session starting at 2.15, which will give us all a chance to have a good rest. There you have it. We're not going to waste any more time. Having said that, I'm going to give the floor to Counsel Kovacic. I think he has a few more minutes of question time left. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, you're right, I have very little time left, but I'm sure we'll get through it in the time you've given us, because I have consulted with my colleagues. I'd like the registrar to have under Sanction, played under Sanction on the monitor some photographs that I'd like to show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I don't have to introduce myself; we started the cross-examination yesterday. I'd like to show you some photographs of Mostar immediately after the Yugoslav army was suppressed from Sarajevo. We haven't seen these in the courtroom yet, and you as the mayor of Mostar and as a real Mostar man born and bred, who I am sure have remembered every bit of destruction the city suffered to tell us whether that is what it was like. We have quite a number of photographs to see and our time is short. I'll just show them one by one slowly, go through them slowly one by one, and then we can comment at the end with a few words. And I'd just like to ask you to tell us to stop if you think that some of the photographs don't relate to that -- that time or that they're not the right photographs. But as I say, I claim that these are photographs of the situation -- depicting the situation in Mostar up until the point the Yugoslav army was pushed out, and the damage that was done during that time when the army attacked Mostar. So that, then, is the old bridge. We've seen that. Perhaps just a brief comment. Yesterday we said that there was some sort of protection, protective covering on the bridge. Is that it, for the passers-by, the pedestrians?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The old bridge once again. This is Kula Tara right next to the old bridge?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's part of the old bridge, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On the other side?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a broader view, depicting one of the towers. And this is the approach to the road towards the old bridge.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)Kujundziluk, this is right next to the bridge?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the approach road with ancient shops which lead directly onto the old bridge itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is that the same quarter?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same quarter, and this is a characteristic building and room from which you could see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. Mr. Registrar, I would like to have the following line struck: From lines 1, 2, 3 and 4 from page 4. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, this is the same quarter.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's it. It's difficult to identify the exact location, but, yes, indeed that is part of the area leading up to the road and bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The same quarter?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a detail, in greater detail. It's the other side, once you've crossed over the old bridge. The same thing again. And this is a little further away from the old bridge. New housing blocks, residential buildings in Donja Mahala. This is the school in Donja Mahala. That's the railway bridge in Bacevici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We spoke about bridges yesterday and you said that all the bridges except for the old bridge had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I think there were seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this is the railway bridge. And the air force bridge, as it was called. Hasan Brkic bridge. Hasan Brkic bridge from another angle. Once again Hasan Brkic bridge, a detail of it.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is Lucki bridge, one of the old bridges built during the Austro-Hungarian times. This is the central bridge in the centre of Mostar. Yes, that's the same bridge on the other side. This is the Carinski bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What side was Carinski bridge on in relation to the old bridge; upstream, downstream?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upstream from the old bridge you have Tito's bridge, Carinski bridge -- no. Yes, and Lucki bridge. So I think that would be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the railway bridge to the north, on the railway line running to Sarajevo. And the bridge in Vojna. This bridge served as a communication line between two settlements in the northern valley of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean north of town?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, north of town. This is the Neretva Hotel, along Tito's bridge, which we saw a moment ago that was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that's the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the centre of town. It's called Musala. And in times past, it was the central square. And this is an annex to the Neretva Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That was destroyed as well, as we can see.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a newly built hotel, the last new hotel that Mostar built. This is Hotel Bristol. There's an old part to the hotel. This is the new part. It is across the water from the Neretva, and the two hotels were linked by Tito's bridge. This is the Hit department store. It was a hit, if I can put it that way; a modern department store.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now we've seen all the bridges -- not bridges, I'm sorry, I meant hotels. Was there any large hotel left standing that wasn't bombed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the sense of a classical hotel but only as an old people's home, and it's called Hotel Ero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. We're going to see a few other buildings. This is the department store and the commercial centre.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the commercial centre, the shopping mall that was built. This is a more modest department store.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. What's this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the street called Mostarski Bataljon in the centre of Mostar, and mostly all the buildings in the centre had shops downstairs on the ground floor. And living quarters upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. This is the same area, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is the primary school that is a little more to the north of the Neretva and Bristol Hotels. This is -- it says "Kirurgija," but we call this the new hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We're going to see a number of hospital buildings, but we have not included those that suffered minor damage. So I'm just going to ask you something about this set of buildings. This is the new hospital, as you said. This is the health centre, Dom Zdravlja. Now, do you happen to remember other medical institutions that suffered damage?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- I don't think any building was left intact, but I can't tell you what all the damage to the different buildings was now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have a few religious buildings. This is the Mekteb.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the symphonic orchestra building, musical institution of late, used that way. And this is the interior of that same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We once again have Marsal Tito Street?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We called that one of our main streets. This is part of the Marsal Tito Street in the south of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We see a whole series of houses that have been completely destroyed. Now, was that at the beginning of the conflict or, rather, the beginning of the attack by the Yugoslav People's Army or what?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, this says the building of the military command.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that particular name, but I do know that that was the building we had held our Assemblies in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean the Municipal Assembly meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think that at some time during history that building might have been called the military command building.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But when it was destroyed, it was the municipal administration building?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the municipal administration building and the Assembly hall where the Assembly sessions were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that the same building?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the same building but viewed from the other side. This is the Svjetlost bookstore, which might have been across the road from the previous building we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an old school once again in that same street, Marsal Tito Street. You can see it on the map today. And this is another building there. This is a building that has been renovated. It is right along the old bridge and you can see how it's been reconstructed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It's also the Mekteb?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And today it is a museum in Herzegovina. And this is a building that we used, we had financial -- part of our financial administration there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The social accounting service?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the social accounting service and other financial offices. Now, this is the Razvitak department store. It was a mixed-purpose building. On the ground floor there was a department store and above that there were apartments. Due to the force of the destruction and explosion, there was a big fire and now none of the top floors exist. They all had to be knocked down. So you'll be able to see the department store on the ground level and then all the rest cleared. And this is another shop in Marsal Tito Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is the railway station in the same street, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's at the beginning of Marsal Tito Street. Well, not really the beginning, but we refer to that whole area as Tito's Street, and this railway station is at an entrance where the new railway station was built and the bus station. And that's still in a pretty bad state. It doesn't look this bad as it does on the photograph, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is another residential building.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is also residential building on Tito's Street also. Now, this is our historic square, Musala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I request to go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. We're in open session. You have a photo before you. To the best of your recollections, can you date this destruction, destruction done to this building? What year would that be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say with precision. But I should like to again refer to this document on the ecocide and urbicide of the area of the city of Mostar, and there one can find in very explicit and detailed terms all the facts about the urbicide which occurred after the pull-out or, rather, the expulsion of the Yugoslav People's Army from the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is hard to make such a distinction, a temporal one, but, Witness, today when we started looking through these photographs, I asked you that if you knew that some of these photographs referred to some destruction in the later stages of the war, to say so.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with precision. I cannot give you an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let us go on and see whether these are the buildings that are in question. When we went through the bridges --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as the bridges are concerned, I can say that they were destroyed during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: About the Old Mostar zone, did you say that that was also devastated during the conflict? Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know what building this is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say "the conflict," which conflict are you referring to, between which two sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are referring now to a period of conflicts between the defensive forces of Mostar and the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the Yugoslav army; interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is the Vakufski Dvor, the Vakufski mansion, the Brace Fejica Street. What part of the city is this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This goes on from the very centre, the very core of downtown Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The magistrate's and the police building in the same section, in the same street?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This was in the period while you were mayor of the city. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had the land registry in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And it was destroyed during the attack of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You were the mayor of the city at the time. Do you recall that the building in which one of your administrative sections was was actually destroyed, and you cannot date it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I cannot, simply because you are asking me to give you a bit of information that I just cannot give you from -- I cannot glean from the overall wholesale tragedy which befell Mostar. I cannot pinpoint that particular bit of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, but, Mr. Gagro --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Counsel Kovacic asked you a very precise question. He said you were the mayor of the town, and there's a building here that is next to the magistrate's office and police, and it was destroyed, and you say, yes, it was destroyed, and then you added a detail, and you said, "In that building we had the land registry department." Now, counsel is asking you who bombed that building and caused the destruction, and then you say, "I don't know." Now, at the time, you yourself were the mayor. Who was the aggressor in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Yugoslav army was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Could there have been anybody else apart from the Yugoslav army that could have been doing damage of this kind at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Then by deduction, a process of deduction, who caused this destruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that happened in that particular period, it could only have been the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The same section, the shops in this street, do you know at what time that was shelled?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The same part of the city, the same zone.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you assist us, Mr. Witness? As a born and bred man from Mostar, you obviously had many acquaintances and friends and so on, and someone was deprived of their house, of their car, of their other property every minute in that period. So could you please help us by referring to such events in order to try and recall the exact period. Of course I'm aware that it is difficult for you to exactly know the time each particular building was destroyed or blown up, but you lived there, and you are perfectly able to associate these events or to place a date on some of them.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I repeat, you insist on a detail for a specific destroyed structure, one building, whereas Mostar suffered a wholesale catastrophe, a global one, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. And precisely that catastrophe, we can see that the city was in a terrible state.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, and this is what I said initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And I agree, but I'm trying to actually define the situation up to the point when the defensive forces of Mostar expelled the Serbs from Mostar, including their artillery, and prevented further damage from occurring. I'm trying to depict a situation in which you were the mayor and that you yourself described for us yesterday. I'm trying to describe the circumstances under which this happened. So please try and link these things. I know that it is difficult. And please do try to recall some of the events at least for some of the buildings depicted in some of these pictures, whether they were destroyed in the first wave.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why do you not accept -- would you not accept this explanation that I'm giving you, that we have documents, photographs of each destroyed building, and we presented that in a study which the city offered under the title "Urbicide of the City of Mostar"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As regards that particular paper, my Defence team has used different sources. The variety of sources are precisely from that paper that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you could have actually specified precisely the documents that the paper identifies and the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We could have done that, and we will be able to do all sorts of things, Mr. Witness, but please, I'm only trying to make the best use of your presence here as a witness for you to assist us on the -- in discussing the subject at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, yes, we have someone on their feet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Drawing on my poor experience from some of the previous sessions, please keep track of the time because I don't want to have my Defence team constrained in terms of time, and please stick to the agreed schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Bear that in mind, Counsel Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I accept this objection, but I actually could not have assumed that discussions of this sort would have come, about especially as refers the sources of materials. I thought that the witness was aware what the sources were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But all right then. So your position is the same in respect of any future photographs I might show you. You are quite certain that they -- so, please, if you are certain that they were destroyed at the time that I imply, please just confirm that. This is the Mujaga Komadina building. Also in the centre of the building, the Herzegovina building in the centre. Do you remember when that building was destroyed? Let us go on. These are residential blocks. Where is Crnica settlement relative to the city?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is on the right bank across from the Brothers Fejic. This is the central zone but on the right bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So these are a couple of industrial facilities and buildings. Yesterday you mentioned the damage they had suffered too. Extensively. This is the main post office on Mose Pijade Street, the residential building in the Carina settlement. Also the same settlement, other residential buildings; the youth centre Rondo, that is in the Rondo area; the archives of Herzegovina that is at Mejdan; the residential and office building, also in Mejdan. The residential and office building in Avenija.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say about this one because we were there on the -- all the Crisis Staff -- or the Crisis Staff was there, rather, so it is possible for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This one, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is actually proof that we were shelled there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And who did the shelling?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav army did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That -- that is -- this is in the vicinity, the Tekija -- is it in the vicinity, this residential building in Tekija?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. The Luka residential quarter?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the southern part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Luka again, the residential buildings, residential buildings of 1st of May, residential buildings in the Semovac settlement. The office and living quarters in the same zone. The residential and administrative building in the same zone. The Kresin Sokak, which part of Mostar that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the old party of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Also residential quarters. Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is the same area of the housing building of the residential buildings. Now here we have Balinovac. What part of town is that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the Western part, extreme western district of Mostar, towards Citluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this exit towards Citluk and Siroki Brijeg is an important road, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is the Cim building. It's a catering establishment. Can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This road was the only communication that the town was left with. If you wanted to go outside the town under siege, and 500 metres up towards there are serpentines. It's a hairpin bend road and this is an area where the Yugoslav army held positions or held -- targeted all those wanting to enter and exit the town, and as I said yesterday, 15 civilians were killed in that way, 15 citizens of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As we can see, a series of buildings were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the buildings in that vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is Jesenica.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jesenica to the south, the southern reaches. Near today's Heliodrom. And you have the airport opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have more photographs to show, religious buildings, commercial buildings, but we need 15 more minutes of time for that. I don't want to take that time for the -- from the other Defence teams, although I think that it would be important for us to see, but we'll find a different occasion. But I'd like to tell you that on page 3 at the beginning of the transcript, line 13, it should read, or we should be more precise, and it says the army, reference was made to the army, whereas it was the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, as is the usual term used. Or abbreviation, if you like. Mr. Gagro, thank you for cooperating. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The next Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll go next, Mr. President, and I'll try to be somewhat brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. From looking at the photographs, Mostar looked a little bit like Dresden after World War II.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer, please. The interpreters could not hear him. Could the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what happened when the last attack took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now, from looking at the -- from looking at the photographs, it would appear that, at least at that particular time in Mostar, not a whole lot of things were --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not getting the image on my screen. Do I need to press a button or something?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Probably you need to press LiveNote, but I don't know if -- perhaps you could be assisted. I'm not going to be referring to photographs. I just want to talk a little bit about what we saw. It would appear to me that at that particular time in Mostar life was pretty hard.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Looks like maybe you didn't have electricity all the time.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, we did our best to see that the utilities were functioning, including electricity, until there was such large-scale destruction that we were just not able to ensure that they were functioning. Now, if I might be allowed to add. I know that in our attempts the Yugoslav People's Army blocked our main transformer station supplying Mostar with electricity, and in an attempt to have it repaired, we asked the international observers to help us out. And when we were approaching that facility, when a representative of the international community appeared in white, dressed in white, he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it, along with electricity, you could say the same thing for running water; that wasn't available all the time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were lucky, because the main supply and the drinking water supply came from the western side, from the Cim area, so that we were able to ensure proper supplies for the town. It was only where -- in the areas where the bridges were destroyed that we weren't able to resume water supplies for that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's right. That would have been for the other side, for the east side.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the other side. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to clarify a couple of points that were mentioned yesterday and today as well with respect to your position at the time. You told us yesterday that there were elections, and as a result of the elections you were a member of the Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand the system as it worked back then, then members of the Assembly would vote among themselves for various candidates, and of course, as a result of those elections among the Assembly members who were elected, you were elected president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the coalitions were already well known; who had the majority in parliament, in the Assembly, and who had the possibility of being elected, and that's how the candidates were put forward. And I said that the three national parties, HDZ, SDA, and SDS, had formed a coalition following the example of the same way of organisation for the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mostar entered into a coalition which -- the HDZ of Mostar entered into a coalition with the SDA and SDS, and they won the majority - 65 per cent - and they thought they could put forward their candidates with realistic possibilities for them becoming the top men in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now, I just want to stick on -- discuss a little bit about the technical aspects of your position and the other positions, because there may have been some misunderstanding created yesterday when they kept referring to you as mayor of Mostar. You, sir, were actually the president of the Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, below the Assembly you have the Executive Board; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Executive Board has a president?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The president is more like the mayor as opposed to the president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he wasn't given those competencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now I just want to explain a little bit as I understand it from my work when I was up in Brcko and I had an understanding of how the system was working. As I know it - and correct me if the system was different in Mostar - at that particular time, the -- the Executive Board was responsible for coming up with a plan as far as what legislation should be drafted. Of course it would be coordinated with the Assembly, but that was part of the Executive Board's responsibility through their departments; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. They proposed certain decisions which we verified, and then they would implement them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now, when you say "we," that would be the Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you as the president of the Assembly, unlike, say, in other countries, you didn't have any real special powers other than one vote like everyone else; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Of course there has to be a president or at least somebody who would represent the Assembly, and that would you as the president.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I was called the first among equals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. And you could say the same thing about the -- the president of the Executive Board. He was first among equals as well, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in the sphere of his authorisation and remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. And being first among equals doesn't mean that you get to make decisions on your own that would affect everyone else; right? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- now that we've clarified that and now that we know that you weren't the mayor and we know a little bit about what the functions of the president of the Assembly are, I want to talk about the Crisis Staff. As I understand it - and again, correct me if I'm wrong - as I understand it, the law as it existed back then provided for a situation where a Crisis Staff could be created in the event of emergency situations.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was always assessed as to how far the institutions of power and authority in a local community could function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But in other words, it wasn't something that you would have to improvise, you'd have to -- it wasn't something that you had created, this Crisis Staff. It was already built into the system and, in time of need, it would activate itself; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the whole purpose of having a Crisis Staff is so that you don't have a hundred Assemblymen, as you would have in Mostar, trying to make a decision, because decisions need to be made on a rather quick basis; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say - and again, correct me if I'm wrong - that while the Crisis Staff is operating, for all intents and purposes the Assembly is no longer functioning as it were, or as it had been.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure we're all clear, that's all. All right. Now, you told us yesterday that your understanding and belief and memory, sometime around the middle of February of 1992 the Crisis Staff was established; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, normally speaking, the Crisis Staff would be composed of the president of the Assembly, the President of the Executive Board, the chief of police, maybe the chief of the Territorial Defence, and maybe a few others; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In this instance, if I understood you correctly, you indicated that in Mostar, along with you there were members of the various political parties. And I mention this because I couldn't help but notice Mr. Hadziosmanovic's name there. Ismet. I'm sure you know him very well. He was a member of the Crisis Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he was the head of the regional SDA party but also, you know, the president of the SDA for Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And normally someone holding that position, being the party leader and with all its responsibilities, normally they don't have an executive role to play; in other words, being a member of the Executive Board. They have other functions, party functions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to talk a little bit about -- go through very quickly, if we could, some of these decisions just so we can have a sense of what was happening. And before I do that, I just want to see if you would agree with the gentleman that testified here before, someone by the name of Pejanovic. He testified in open court. He lived on the east side. He was a fireman. He was the head of the fire department. You might even know him.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And he had indicated that it was around the 11th of May, 1992, that he left the east side, but in actuality, it was around the 13th or so of May, 1992, when -- when more or less the east side was overrun by the JNA and everyone crossed over, more or less, to the west side. Would that be correct, the timing of it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me what it was he said exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, he had indicated that at least he left his post on the 11th of May because of the heavy attack, and around the 13th or so people were fleeing. And in fact, during some rather brilliant cross-examination from Mr. Praljak, if I may say so, he brought out the fact that folks as they were fleeing from the east to the west were actually jumping into the Neretva and having to swim over. There was that kind of a panic going on as they were trying to get away from the JNA forces that were attacking. Would that be a correct assessment of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, having that date in mind, I want to fast forward a little bit, or go back a little bit. As I understand it -- I have a decision here that appears -- you signed, and if we could have it on the ELMO -- or on the e-court, I apologise. It's 1D 00494. It's a decision dated 12 December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't have it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to wait, okay? I'm just giving you sort of the warm-up. When you -- do you see it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I read the whole -- see the whole document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sure. And I even have a hard copy for you if you like.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you see the -- do you see your name there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So there is no dilemma that you are the author of this particular document, or you signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this is a decision dated 12 April, 1992, where you in your capacity as the commander of the Crisis Staff establish -- or you appoint a commander for the Territorial Defence of Mostar, and the gentleman's name is Hasic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it would be fair to say, would it not, if we look at the preamble, it says that this is pursuant to a decision by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it's dated 9 April, 1992. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it - and correct me if I'm wrong - that perhaps you waited so long in making this appointment because you were waiting for some sort of a decision from the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was located in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But if I understood you correctly, the JNA came in in November or December of 1991 and all hell was breaking loose -- or September. And if we go on, September, October, November, December, January, February, March, and it's not until April that the good folks in Sarajevo wake up and decide that folks in Mostar should activate the Territorial Defence and appoint a commander; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now -- rather strange, don't you think, that they would wait all this long?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we just followed orders from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. But what I'm saying is rather strange that the folks back in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to ask the gentlemen who functioned that way over there. You'd have to ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it around this time, too, all hell is breaking loose around Sarajevo, too, because they're under siege, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to say that we'd already lost all the weapons we had, that the Territorial Defence had of the Municipal Assembly of Mostar at that time. The JNA had already done its best to take our last bullet, the last bullet that we had in our warehouses as a reserve to activate the Territorial Defence. And let me also add that the citizens had bought all that with their own money, purchased it all with their own money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, might I have -- might I have a clarification, because I'm a bit confused. On line 14, the question says that at that time finally they, the folks in Mostar, appoint a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That gives the idea that this document is appointing a commander. As I read the translation of the document, the document authorises the commander, who already exists, to name aides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Maybe I'm wrong, so I would like you to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it could be that you're absolutely correct, but let's go through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A Territorial Defence existed prior to this point in time; correct? I mean, I don't want to get into a long discussion about the All People's Defence and what have you, but in essence a Territorial Defence would have existed in every municipality including the Mostar municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Through this document, through this decision, it says here that you're authorising this gentleman, Hasic, to appoint his aides and other workers. Was Hasic at that particular time, was he already the commander of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether we in the Crisis Staff had already proclaimed Hasic commander of the Municipal Staff, if this decision refers just to the fact that he should appoint and put forward his co-workers, which was necessary for them to be able foundation properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So can I take it at least -- can I take -- can I understand this decision at least to reflect the fact that even if Hasic was a commander at the time, he did not have the requisite aides in order to carry on the functions of a -- of the Territorial Defence of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that we could activate our Territorial Defence -- or, rather, had we been able to do that, everything would have functioned differently. But we were left with just 200 active policemen who carried weapons. All the rest was beyond our reach.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But I guess -- and I -- I just want to draw a couple of points on this. One, your decision is based on a decision that was made in Sarajevo at the Presidency level 9 April, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We already know that as early as September, 1991, the winds of war are blowing in a southerly fashion from the Republic of Croatia, and they're coming down to Mostar; right? Not to mention there are some other ones raging from south to north, you know, or from other directions, because even Sarajevo is under siege at this point; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that I agree with what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I -- and I guess I'm asking whether you find it rather strange that Alija Izetbegovic, the president of the Presidency, who is supposed to be in charge of this country and looking after the welfare of everyone, including the Croats, why on earth is he waited until 9 April, 1992, to react?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Several objections. I realise this is cross-examination, but for a long time now these questions have been overly argumentative. Counsel's putting his -- making his closing argument rather than putting questions to the witness. Secondly, as Mr. Karnavas has said the last couple of days, this question assumes facts not in evidence. There is no evidence whatsoever about what Mr. Izetbegovic was doing during this time, no evidence. So what Mr. Karnavas has just said is nothing more than a wild assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we know from the witness that nothing was done be Mr. Izetbegovic. I merely asked if he knew. Now, if the gentleman doesn't know, I'll move on. Maybe we'll hear it from Mr. Kljujic or some other witness, but I'm perfectly happy to move on if the Court feels that the Prosecutor's objection should be sustained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to clarify this question, this decision that you signed where the commander of the Territorial Defence of Mostar is authorised to appoint aides, people to help him in his tasks, you signed this decision on the 12th of April. However, after that, in this same document, refer to a decision of the Presidency of -- in the preamble of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the integration of all forces in the republic. Now, was that not linked to the creation and establishment of the BH army, which led to the fact that in fact the Territorial Defence was included into the BH army? Was this not -- decision not taken in that context? Can you explain that to me, please? Because in your decision, you refer to the decision of the Presidency, which we don't have in front of us, but you also mention the fact that it has to do with the unification of all the armed forces, because the proclamation of a state of war had already been made. So wasn't this the moment when you were pooling all available resources? So you as the signatory, what can you tell me about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We just did the job and assignment that we received from the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But that doesn't say -- tell me anything to execute assignments. Which ones, pursuant to this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no. I think it was more a formal matter. It just stated matters officially. We knew what we had to do. The Territorial Defence didn't exist any more. The people existed, but there were no weapons. We didn't have the weaponry that we ought to have had, so it was all too late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But could you look at the document in B/C/S, please, because the English document, the English version, don't seem to reflect what it says in the B/C/S. I looked at the addressees, the list of addressees of your decision, and in the B/C/S document we see that you were sending copies to MNO Sarajevo. After that it says MUP BiH Sarajevo, and then RSTO Sarajevo. Whereas in the English version, in the English translation, it says -- ah, yes, I see, it's on the second page. I should have looked on the second page. Yes. Right. But anyway, this order, you were informing Sarajevo about it because it was an important order; isn't that right? Otherwise, why would you have informed Sarajevo about the order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we were just fulfilling our obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So addressee number 5, MNO, what is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the Ministry of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There you have it, the National Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Ministry of Internal Affairs is the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Fine. If you were informing the Ministry of National Defence in Sarajevo, that means that your decision was related to the question of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I hope to clear up a lot of this, because I dare say, with all due respect, there were some assumptions perhaps that were made in the questions posed that do not -- are not reflected in some of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's take it a step back. I just happen to have this proclamation of immediate threat of war, okay? Perhaps we can put it on the ELMO -- oh, it's already in. I apologise. It's 3D 00275. Perhaps we can see it. And I have a copy --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Take it easy. [In English] Okay. We don't -- apparently we don't have it in B/C/S, but I'm sure we have some fantastic translators and interpreters who are assisting us, and they could help us out here. So perhaps I can read slowly, and it could be translated for the gentleman. Sir, this is -- if we look at the bottom, it says -- we have a date 8 April, 1992. If we go to the top, we see it's from the Official Gazette. The preamble reads: "Pursuant to provisions of amendments ... of the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and on the recommendation of the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at a session held on 8 April, 1992, issued the following: "Decision on the proclamation of an immediate threat of war. "I. An immediate threat of war is hereby proclaimed in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Mind you, again, this is 8 April, 1992, and you've already indicated - not just you but others - that the JNA had been actively engaging in war activities in Bosnia as early as September. We'll go on. "II. During the immediate threat of war, the Presidency of the RBH shall be expanded to include the Chairman of the RBH Assembly, the RBH Prime Minister, and the Commander of the Territorial Defence of the Republic." Sounds like they're establishing a Crisis Staff themselves, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then we go to Article III: "During the immediate threat of war, the RBH Presidency shall issue decrees with force of law and decisions on appointments and dismissals which will be submitted for approval to the RBH Assembly as soon as it is able to meet." These are emergency measures that are normally taken; right? These are normally taken under emergency situations; right? Now, I take it --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take it it is based on this that you then ask, in your decision, for Mr. Hasic -- you say, "... is hereby authorised to appoint his aides and other workers necessary -" and I underscore that word "necessary" - "for the functioning of the Mostar municipal Territorial Defence Staff." Now, from that it would -- I mean, if we use a little logic, I can only suspect that the Mostar Municipal Territorial Defence was not in fact functioning, which is why you're issuing this decision based on what the folks in Sarajevo have done for him to get going and appoint the necessary personnel for the functioning of the Territorial Defence; right? Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't get the translation on that. I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't have the state of facts clearly presented to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Well, and as you've indicated, by this point all the weapons from the Territorial Defence have been taken, so it's a bit like closing the door -- the barn door after the horses have run out, if you get my expression.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what it is that you're targeting at, and that was objectively so, but what can one do? Life was a quite different matter, and we were forced to organise ourselves in a different fashion altogether, organising ourselves as we were enjoined upon to do, and of course we had to handle the everyday situations as best as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand it, and, sir, don't think for one moment that I do not appreciate the difficult situation that you were in, nor am I being critical. I'm just bringing out certain facts that were brought upon you, not that you created. Now, if I could look at -- if we could look at another document, because now we have -- we have a decision to Hasic. If we could look at 1D 00495. Here - and this may help with one of the questions raised by the president -- okay. I'm told that we cannot find it. We have it for the ELMO in your language. Okay. Here it is. All right. If you could just sort of rest your eyes on this document a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We see that the date is 17 April, 1992. So that is five days after you've already made the decision. Okay. It takes Mr. Hasic five days in the middle of this chaos, in the middle of this emergency going on, it takes him five days and he makes his appointments, and could you tell us, sir, where does he send this notice to?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, to the Republican Territorial Defence Staff of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Republican Territorial Defence Staff, sent by the Municipal Staff of Mostar, the Territorial Defence Municipal Staff of Mostar about these appointments, according to our order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that republican staff, is that in Sarajevo, by any chance, or is that in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not in Mostar. It is in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the institutions of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were concentrated in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So if I get this -- if I get it right, you issue a decision being the Crisis Staff commander for Mr. Hasic, and then Mr. Hasic, after waiting five days, makes his appointments, doesn't notify you and instead notifies Sarajevo. Is that -- is that what I can conclude from this document? Because I don't see you on the mailing list.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably wasn't that important that we should be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You don't think it was important?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that that particular segment of the defence of Mostar could not function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Which then brings us to the April 29th decision, because by this point it would appear that you're reaching out to the only available realistic option, and that is the HVO; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And, actually, we said so by our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. So -- and you could see why I'm bringing these out. You see, I'm stringing it along because it seems by the 29th you have no choice, and in fact, thank God, there is an option out there to assist in the defence of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I'm going to object to the argumentative nature of these questions. This is argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this decision, and this is P 0 -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [Interpretation] It mentions the members of the STO and the fact that they were changed. Does this mean that -- yes, it's working now. It says there's the former OPSTO, and there's a list of 13 individuals. Does this mean -- this means -- or does this mean that the former one was still functioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it does. Formally, yes. The appointment of new people had not been resolved, but it was reorganised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this body was restructured.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And since you brought us to that point, I guess maybe I should spend a little more time on this document. Again, 1D 00495.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at the first seven names that Mr. Hasic appoints, he puts himself first as the commander. Then we see chief of staff. That's a pretty important position. Chief of security, medical service, quartermaster service, financial service, personnel and mobilisation. It seems to me that if he had to appoint all these people, that Territorial Defence, for all intents and purposes, was on paper only and wasn't functioning; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And is it not correct, sir, that you as the commander of the Crisis Staff, along with the other members of the Crisis Staff, should know of these appointments and should be kept abreast of what the Territorial Defence is doing, because after all, it's based on your authorisation, your decision, that he's having to make these appointments; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, our decision. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And based -- at least based on this piece of paper that we have - again, 1D 00495, Mr. Hasic's appointment list - it would appear that you are not served with a copy and you are not notified even though you are in Mostar, Sarajevo is under siege, and somehow he manages to communicate with Sarajevo but doesn't have the wherewithal to communicate with you, the commander of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I'm going to object and this time let me illustrate exactly the point very specifically. The witness already answered the previous question. If you look at page 39, line -- line 14, Mr. Karnavas puts the same question, he's just put this question, and at line 20 the witness answers "Yes, our decision. That's correct." The question has been answered. Everything that follows after that is simply an argument by Mr. Karnavas. Now, I object. I know it's cross-examination, but I object to continued argument. The witness answered the question and then Mr. Karnavas makes a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is proper cross-examination. I'm trying to assist the Trial Chamber here. But I'll move on to the next decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we have the decision on the 29th, and since we're running out of time, I don't want to take the time on going through the preamble, but obviously there is a preamble there which sets out the reasons why you're having to issue this decision; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But one cannot help but notice that in this preamble you notify, or you alert everybody, the whole public, that the decision is made in part because Mostar is under partial occupation; right? It's right in the preamble that Mostar is under partial occupation.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, it was. It had been; right? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were very realistic in appraising the situation that we had found ourselves in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Right. Now, we -- I don't want to spend too much time in here with this document, but if we look at it very briefly, you obviously -- I want to focus a little bit on point VIII, more specifically the very last or the second to last article. It says: "The crisis --"

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I have it on my screen again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's P 00180. I apologise. I'm labouring under this new technology. Okay. That's not it yet. We're going to get to it.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe that's it.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What item did you say I should look at?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Item VIII. We can see it right here. Right there.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item VIII, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll read the English and follow along. If you need to correct my translation, you go ahead. "The crisis headquarters of the municipality of Mostar shall -" I underscore the word "shall" - "establish as soon as possible the temporary Executive Council which will ensure the functioning of the government bodies of the Assembly of the municipality of Mostar." Right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was logical, because with its number, the Crisis Staff could hardly service the overall requirements of life in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I totally understand you. And we have the nine members. But, you know, it strikes me a little bit -- I must say a little odd that assuming -- assuming your memory serves you right that the Crisis Staff was established as early as February 15 - on or about - 1992, here we are April 29th and it's only through this decision that the Crisis Staff at least recognises that it needs to set up a temporary Executive Council. I'm sure there is some reason, but you can see that perhaps there was a lag of time between the establishment of the Crisis Staff and this decision.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, we had not been aware of how long the crisis situation would last. And had it been able to resolve it over a short period of time, there would have been no need to transform the basic structures which actually managed the functioning of the city and its life. And that is what we had been expecting, that things would calm down, that this calamity would bypass us. So we waited for the nick of time, as it were, to actually assess that it was indeed necessary to reorganise the structures managing the life in the city, and that is the reason why that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were able to function in peacetime, but under this situation, you were not able to function.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'll have to draw your attention to one fact, and I'm speaking from a personal angle. I did my utmost to establish communication with the Yugoslav army. As part of that, we co-opted into our Crisis Staff the commander of the Mostar garrison, Mr. Pantelic, who was present when difficult situations were being discussed, and we wanted to cooperate with him in order to address certain critical moments, and he was ready to do so. He was very cooperative. But to understand the entire situation, when the Titograd Uzice Corps and its forces arrived, that was absolutely outside the control of our own garrisons. So that communication between General Torbica, who was the commander of that corps and had his command post in Kifino Selo, which is 40 kilometres away from Mostar, so that we were unable to communicate at any time. But through Mr. Pantelic, as our official garrison commander, we had his assistance in establishing such communication. I cannot tell you in detail how that actually evolved, in every single detail, but it was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If I understand you correctly -- and I don't know where we are with the break, but if I can just understand you correctly, don't assume that I'm being critical, because I'm not, but as the events were unfolding, you were doing your utmost to keep danger at bay, negotiating, you know, walking that tightrope, and then at some point, as you say, the Montenegrin reservists come in -- or you say Titograd; I assume that's who you're referring to -- and by that point now you're at the precipice and there is no room to manoeuvre. It seems you were doing your best for several months to try to resolve the situation peacefully and then, all of a sudden, you found yourself with no other choice; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I can say that I'm proud to have been able to manoeuvre for such a long time at the expense of personal misunderstandings, with falling out with many of my associates who didn't appreciate my reasons, because I managed for us to avoid this conflict, and we did this for a long time prior to the Presidency's proclamation of the immediate threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree. I agree, and --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you should be commended by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And right now I think we need to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree. We should have a break now. It's half past ten. We'll have a break until 11.00 since we need a half-hour break for technical reasons. We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I have a few more questions. I'll try to hurry up. Now, getting back to this decision of April 29th, again, if we focus our attention on paragraph VIII, again I just want to make sure that I understand it. What it's calling for is the establishment of an Executive Council which actually would be sort of like an Executive Board to run the day-to-day business of the Mostar municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And -- and of course that's necessary because the Crisis Staff itself can carry out that function.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday we looked at a document. It was P 00190. And this was the document that was a decision issued by the HVO appointing a Special Purpose Council, if you recall that.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, just -- if we could look at this document for a second. It shows that -- first of all, it's dated May 7, so that would be approximately six or seven days after your decision; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And can we assume -- can we assume that in spite of the emergency situation and the raging of the war in Mostar, at least as of May 6th the crisis headquarters had yet to establish an Executive Council as it had mandated in its own decision of 29 April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So even though you told us yesterday you had not seen this particular decision, you nonetheless commented - and correct me if I'm wrong, and I'm going to paraphrase a little bit - you thought, based on what is contained in the document, the tasks that this Special Purpose Council undertakes are vital and necessary under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look -- if we look at some of the names -- for instance, the first name, Neven Tomic, you know who he is. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Prlic of course we talked about, and some of the others, including at the very end we see Camil Salahovic, also known as Limi, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Camil Salahovic, just for those of us who don't know him, was at this point in time the vice-president of the SDA in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain, but I think you might be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would he be a close associate of Mr. Hadziosmanovic at this time and period?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, the names of these people here, if I could use a word, technocrat, would it be fair to say that these individuals bring with them a collective body of knowledge and skills necessary for running the day-to-day affairs as if they were in fact part of an Executive Council as was mandated by the decision of 29 April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say that under item 2, the task of the council for the needs of the Mostar municipal staff in the HVO is as follows -- well, with regards to these tasks, unfortunately it doesn't mention or, rather, it neglects the Crisis Staff of -- the HVO Crisis Staff of Mostar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Fair enough. Be fair to say also that the Crisis Staff has neglected the folks of Mostar because here it is six days later and the HVO is having to at least establish a Special Purpose Council to carry out the functions that the Crisis Staff should have carried out perhaps long before this -- this period.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You could understand it in that way, but I wouldn't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the HVO was entrusted with protecting the city, protecting the citizens, and fending back the JNA and the aggressors, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in doing so obviously they would need resources; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They would need to look to the municipality, to the Crisis Staff, or perhaps to a non-existent Executive Council to provide them at least with the necessary resources to carry out the task that was given to them by the Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Could you just show me a document that they addressed to the Crisis Staff, however, with such request? I would be grateful if you could do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree with you on that, but then again you must show me a document where the Crisis Staff establish an Executive Council. Because again, if we could go back - and I don't want to be critical - but if the Crisis Staff was established back in February 15, 1992, as a result of a crisis, and here it is April 29 we have a decision, and then as late as May 7th still there is no Executive Council, you would agree with me at least there is a need -- there is a need for a Special Purpose Council, especially - especially - when the town is in essence in flames, is burning.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
