utterances.text: I'd like to tell you about how I perceive these events. It's not as if we didn't have any resources, you know. With this decision, we would just verify to confirm all the functions that were essential in order to make sure that the town was supplied and secure, but throughout the entire period of the Crisis Staff's activities, certain things functioned properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree with you. And certain things were lacking, and certain things were needed; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we can argue about the establishment of the Special Purpose Council, but you in fact, sir, indicated that what it was tasked to do was vital and necessary under the circumstances. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness please speak up when answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You have to speak up a little bit. You have a very soft voice.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, just to remind ourselves, this is May 7th. The next document that we looked at yesterday was dated May 15, 1992, and -- and this is P 00209. Now, we have it in the system, however, I would kindly request to put the -- a cleaner copy in your language on the ELMO, because I think the preamble is hard to read. Perhaps with this clean copy, and of course if it -- first we'll look at it. We'll see if it is a true and accurate copy, if it reflects that which it is supposed to reflect, and then I'll ask you some questions. Okay. Now, if you could look at it, sir. Look at it carefully and tell us whether that is the same document that we talked about yesterday, the one that was signed by Jadran Topic. This was the order disbanding the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And would you agree with me at least that at least the copy I provided you - not that I want to take any particular credit - but at least mine is a little bit more readable and you'll be able to at least help us out here. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Having said that, perhaps you could glance at it. And I don't want to go into it in great detail because we'll be able to read it and hopefully we'll have it translated, because I see the English translation is lacking, certain words being illegible, it's fair to say that this preamble, does it not, sir, give us sort of a historical context, a background of what preceded?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and so from this preamble we can see that at least at the state level and, even somewhat at the local level, there is an understanding and perhaps an appreciation that there is a dangerous situation that needs to be rectified and that as a result the HVO has taken it upon themselves to disband the Crisis Staff and to more or less take over the activities; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you base such an assumption on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, remember we started with -- we started with Mr. Pejanovic. May 11th to May 13th he was talking about. And we talked about right around this period of time, because this is May 15th, we talked about people having to swim the Neretva, rather fast and cold body of water, as they're trying to escape from east to west. And it's within this context.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what I'm talking about. So at least you could -- we could agree that one would appreciate the urgency in the situation in trying to establish some sort of working order in Mostar under these most difficult circumstances; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And as I understand it, sometime in June, unlike what the Prosecutor said yesterday that the JNA left, they were chased out; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They were chased out by the HVO and others.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to make sure that there's no misunderstanding on one point, and perhaps I'm the cause of this confusion. At the state level at this particular point in time, at the state level, BiH, such as it was, there is no military force to speak of, is there? There's no, you know, JNA, you know, for BiH; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All we have are Territorial Defences; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in some places, as in Mostar, for instance, first the weapons were siphoned out by the JNA, and virtually these municipalities were left to fend for themselves, to try to protect themselves. So in other words, there's nothing that they can look at in Sarajevo. They may be able to send a telegram to say here is the list of people we're appointing, but in essence Sarajevo can't do anything for Mostar at this period of time; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, that is why -- that is why you reach out on April 29th to the HVO to help out, and indeed they do help out; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Now, I just have a couple of -- a couple of other matters, very quickly. More like a point of clarification, if anything. Yesterday -- yesterday you were reminded by the Prosecution of a particular document. It was a conclusion -- it was a conclusion from the Herzegovina Regional Community, topical regional community meeting that was held on 12 November, 1991. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You attended that -- you attended that meeting. You attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And by the way, I'm speaking of 1D 00487. Now, I've been to some of these meetings. Not party meetings, but I've been to similar kind of meetings where normally a sheet is passed around for all the participants to write their names and maybe even sign their names so we know who was all at the meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the fact that you've signed in that you were present doesn't necessarily mean that that signature carries any weight with respect to any conclusions that were found or purported to have been found later on; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a correct interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you'd put the third page on the ELMO for the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if -- if -- okay. Now, the way -- okay. And that's your signature, by the way, we were talking about, number 22?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And all this signature means --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, Madam Usher, you can just relax. I don't think I'll need you any more for right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But that signature, all it reflects is that you were present; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, normally the meetings that I attend to similar to these sorts of meetings, the first thing that happens is you might have a discussion on whether you're going to adopt the minutes of the previous meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's to make sure that when a conclusion or minutes are drafted later on, post-meeting, that those who might agree to it have an opportunity to read it, analyse it, and make sure before they say yes or no that they know exactly what they're agreeing to or not agreeing to; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness again be asked to speak up because the interpreter is having difficulty in hearing his answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You have to speak up, all right?. Don't be shy around here. We're all friends.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I know that. Now, the last thing I want to point out is this: You're -- assuming you didn't agree to these conclusions, can we also not assume that none of these names that are on this piece of paper necessarily agree or disagree with these conclusions, based on the signature itself on the sign-up sheet?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so -- and I don't want to give away anything because we'll have to wait for other witnesses to come, it might be that we have to wait to see what other documents are generated after this particular meeting to see what, if any, of these conclusions were actually adopted or proposed, adopted, and implemented; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we shall also see who signed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly. Okay. Sir, I want to thank you very, very much. I hope it wasn't too painful.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm reminded, Mr. President, I'm supposed to introduce some documents. There are three documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Do so but rapidly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 00487, 494, 495. Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] The following exhibits are therefore tendered and admitted today with the following references: 1D 00487, 1D 00494, and 1D 00495. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Kovacic, I forgot to mention the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to save time and do this at the end. I also suggest the photographs be given an IC number, and I'll provide the registrar with a CD and hard copy of the photographs, that they can be integrated in the system. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there are no documents you want to deal with?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We have no other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, could you deal with the IC number for the photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The bundle of photographs presented today will bear the reference IC 00021. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have the next Defence team now, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gagro, good morning to you. My name is Vesna Alaburic, attorney from Zagreb, and here I'm Defence counsel for General Milivoj Petkovic. My questions will require a little less time than my colleagues because we've clarified many issues, but before I go ahead with my first question, I'd like us to clear up one of your questions which was recorded on page 12 of the transcript, lines 12 to 16. When Mr. Kovacic showed you photographs from the publication, Uziteit [phoen], you were asked what that publication was and it says here that urbicide occurred after the Yugoslav army had left town. That's what the record says. Now, can you explain to us -- explain this to us? Did you mean that the book was compiled after the army had left Mostar and the book contains photographs of buildings which were destroyed by the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who interpreted this otherwise, but that's the fact as it says. Urbicide is a document compiled after the Yugoslav army was expelled from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, at the time when you were performing your functions in Mostar, did you ever meet General Milivoj Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I can say unfortunately I didn't have the pleasure of meeting him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, during the time that you had -- were going about your functions, did you ever hear of General Milivoj Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Although I like the name, and I assume you know why.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I can well believe that. Now, in view of the fact that you didn't know my client nor did you hear about him during the material time, the time you're telling us about, I'm going to ask you a few questions because I do consider that your knowledge and experience will help us clarify certain parts of the indictment. So I'm just going to make a short introductory address and say that in the indictment and the counts against our clients, it says, first and foremost, that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was proclaimed by extremist nationalist elements of the HDZ of the BiH, and then it goes on to say that with the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna a joint criminal enterprise started of ethnic cleansing and aiding and abetting ethic cleansing of the Muslims, and then it goes on to say that in the joint criminal enterprise members of the municipal members of the organs of power and authority took part as well as member of the HDZ, and all that beginning with November, 1991. So since at that time you held prominent posts in the municipal organs and were a member of the HDZ yourself, I'm going to ask you a few questions in that regard. You told us, and this was recorded yesterday on page 15, line 1, of the transcript, that you supported the idea of a Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, do you consider yourself to be an extreme nationalist of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me when I say that the idea of a Herceg-Bosna was supported by all members of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you also agree with me when I put it to you that the idea of Herceg-Bosna was supported by plebiscite by all Croats living in the areas of the municipalities that are associated into Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in view of the fact that the political party, the Croatian Democratic Union in the indictment in a certain way is said to be an organisation which gave shape to some criminal enterprise, and you were a member of that political party, I'm going to ask you to comment parts of the statute of the Croatian Democratic Union, and may we have the document on e-court. The Prosecution number is 00013. P 00013. And could it be shown -- could we see pages 2 and 3. Pages 2 and 3, and the page begins with the purpose for the establishment of the Croatian Democratic Union of BH. May we have page 2 displayed, please. Perhaps it would be simpler if we were to place the document on the ELMO. May we have the technical booth's assistance. Pages 2 and 3 we need. Thank you, here we have it. In Article 10 of the statute, point 10.1. It says the following, that the HDZ, among other things, will strive for the embodiment of statehood and sovereignty of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that so? Was that how it was, Mr. Gagro?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In point 10.5, it says that the Croatian Democratic Community will strive for the linking up and inclusion of Bosnia-Herzegovina into the European Community of Associated Nations.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the next page, page 3 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they do not have the English version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So we're looking at page 3, point 10.8, which is rather a lengthy point, but there are certain sections which I consider to be very important, so I'll read them out. It says the following: "The HDZ of BiH will endeavour to implement its programme in a legal manner, proposing constitutional, legal, and socio-political changes for the faster emergence from the crisis and the gradual implementation of full parliamentary democracy. The HDZ-BiH is resolutely in favour of including -- having BiH included into the European Community and the modern integration of the world. Everything must be done along those lines to have BiH take part in the Alpe-Adria community and that that should be as efficacious as possible and demand that BiH be accepted into the union of European Regions, ARE. All efforts and goals of the HDZ-BiH should be geared towards realising the social -- to realising social freedoms and justice, morals and work, especially the happiness and well-being of all peoples -- of all people without any differences who consider BiH to be their homeland.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was that how it was, Mr. Gagro?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it was on this basis that we in fact compiled this document, and that's why I supported it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, on the basis of this statute and programmes and principles of this kind, would it be proper to conclude that the political party known as the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina fully wished to see a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina as a member on an equal footing of international associations and the international community in general?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we said that clearly through our statute and you've just read that out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you tell us, please, Mr. Gagro, whether today in Bosnia-Herzegovina political discussions are being held about a unitary set-up for the country?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, is one of the options for a unitary establishment and organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina one of them?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would one of the solutions be the existence of three national entities?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one of the variants as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And is there a third option, to retain the present solution with two entities?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are solutions of that kind being bandied about as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is there another solution linked to a proposal from Republika Srpska to follow the example of Montenegro and organise a referendum, one of the options too?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the latest one, the latest option. And the Serbs having lost Montenegro are proposing that option and exerting pressure on the international community to give some thought to that about Kosovo, a solution for Kosovo, which is looming on the horizon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, tell us, all these concepts, all these options for an internal structure of the country, are discussions being held quite openly about all those as variations, the pros and cons being stressed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. But I think that the situation in the HDZ is seeming to loom up again in the same relationships that existed before this unfortunate conflict, and today too we have divergencies within the HDZ itself over a concept of a solution for the future, that is to say how Bosnia Herzegovina should be established and organised in the future.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down, please, and make pauses between question and answer, thank you, for the benefit of one and all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Not only in the countries of the former Yugoslavia but in other countries too, is it usual that within one political party there are different views of one and the same problem?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That's the democratic principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, Mr. Gagro - and this was recorded on page 48 of the transcript, lines 9 to 11 - there was just one sentence in which you mentioned the contribution of the Bosniaks in raising tensions in Mostar and the entire region as well, and you mentioned that it was only later that you happened to learn that the Bosniaks, too, or, rather, the Muslims at that time, tried to organise themselves and realise some of their goals. Can you clarify what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: Just as we Croats in the HDZ before, and today, too, had differences of opinion and divergent opinions about the political rules and policy to be pursued within a party and in discussions amongst parties, so also the Bosniak side had different options which were not only always unanimously accepted. That is why I said that their options were not always the same and supported by one and all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you be a little more precise and tell us what those options were and who the protagonists of those options were, ones which did not contribute to co-existence between the Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you quite openly, Mr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic, who was president of the Regional Board of the SDA of Mostar was a member of the Crisis Staff, our Crisis Staff. However, the replacement of the Crisis Staff meant that Mr. Hadziosmanovic was replaced too, and the new temporary government - let me put it that way because I don't know what it was actually called - accepted and took in other Bosniaks without the original Bosniaks, the Bosniaks who had originally participated and been members of the Crisis Staff. So that would be an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I followed you there. Did you mean to say that Mr. Hadziosmanovic was somebody who was an extremist and opposed to cooperation?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No; quite the contrary. He was very cooperative. Yes, he was very cooperative until the situation escalated, and he had opponents for other options, and that's why they endeavoured to eliminate him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you name the people who were opponents to Mr. Hadziosmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I would like to name the people and enter into these inter-party debates.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all from me, Mr. Gagro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just a very brief question following on from what you said a moment ago. You said that you regretted not having met General Petkovic and that Mr. -- you had sympathies for Mr. Petkovic. Could you explain those sentiments. You mentioned some sentiments that you had with respect to Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said referred to the fact that we had the same name. So that's why I felt this affinity towards him. We have the same name. But this is the first time I see Mr. Petkovic, here today in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Counsel Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, but just one slight intervention with respect to the transcript. On page 60, line 1, I think there was -- the answer was mistakenly recorded about some topical relationships within the HDZ, so that in line 3 of that answer on page 60, it says: "[In English] ... today too we have divergent SIS within the HDZ ..." [No interpretation]. [Interpretation] It's been recorded as SIS, S-I-S, which is a secret service, intelligence service. That's wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's not SIS, it's divergencies, the plural, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, would you like to tender any documents? The statute and the HDZ document, would you like to have that tendered? And there are several articles within that statute. You were referring to just certain parts, beginning with Article 8. We don't have articles 8 to 7 -- 1 to 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like this, Your Honour: The statute was adopted as Prosecution Exhibit P 00013 and we already discussed it. We discussed it when we listened to expert witness Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So that document is already in evidence, and the number is P 13. Thank you. The next Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Gagro, I'm going to be asking you several questions as Defence counsel for Mr. Valentin Coric. Yesterday during your testimony, and today too, in describing the situation in Mostar at the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, you said that the situation was fairly chaotic as far as the functioning of the town was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that the level of destruction of the town was considerable, and I'm talking about destruction during the Greater Serbia occupation or occupation by the Yugoslav People's Army and the struggle of the town to defend itself and become liberated.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exact -- that's exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we see document 5D now 01091. If we don't have it in the e-court, then perhaps we can put it on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you see that document, Mr. Gagro? You can probably see it in its entirety, and we can all see it partially. This is a comment of General Perisic of 19 of April, 1992, which instructs the artillery units of the Yugoslav army to shell targets in the city; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the targets which are indicated here under item 2 are in fact civilian targets. These are parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Cim, Ilici?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes; Cim, Ilici, Donji Brijeg, Bijeli Brijeg, Donja Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: These are city sections?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the 19th of April was Easter according to the new calendar, it was the Catholic Easter. Do you remember that the shelling took place on that Easter day?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There have been so many instances of shelling that I really couldn't tell whether it was Easter or any other day for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Tell me, at that time in that period, which is to say March and April, 1992, as the Crisis Staff president you met on a number of occasions with UNPROFOR representatives, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: These meetings with UNPROFOR, however, did not yield much fruit, so that on the 29th of April a decision was adopted whereunder the Crisis Staff was entrusting the HVO with the defence of the city; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: One of the signatories of that document is Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic as well?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic at that time was the president of the city organisation, the municipal organisation of the SDA of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose also of the regional one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: The regional one as well, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the registrar please display on the ELMO document 5D 01092, please. We can't see it in electronic form, but we can physically display it, show it to you. We have the English translation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagro, in the short period did you manage to see what this is about, this short time? This is Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic who introduces himself as a member of the Crisis Staff, addressing the citizens of Mostar precisely on that date, the 29th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This clearly speaks about the decision that we signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So this is Dr. Hadziosmanovic commenting on Radio Mostar the reasons for the adoption of that decision.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and explaining to the public why it was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at page 1, halfway down the middle, you will see that he explains also the differences in the ways that -- in the response of the Muslims and the response of the Croats to the occupation of Mostar. Can you find that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So it is a fact that the Croatian people was aware that this would indeed happen one day, whereas the Muslims didn't have a clue.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were aware, because they participated together with us in the city structures given the situation that obtained and the organisation of the Muslims at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So we can describe Mr. Hadziosmanovic at that time as the leader of the most influential and strongest Muslim party?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So in this statement that he read out on Radio Mostar he actually acknowledged that the Muslims were unprepared for what had befallen them?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you look at page 2 of this statement or, rather, of this communique for the public, Dr. Hadziosmanovic comments on the position of the Territorial Defence. As yesterday and today we referred to it repeatedly, do -- are we agreed, Mr. Gagro, that Dr. Hadziosmanovic, in the fourth and fifth line of page 2, refers to the JNA as the political and military aggressor and a part of the armed formations which are subsumed under the concept of the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Territorial Defence that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Inherited, you mean inherited.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Because this is the Territorial Defence which was inherited from the Yugoslav system and was predominantly, do we agree, in Serbian hands, therefore the leadership was predominantly Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about the Mostar TO, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: No, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will both of you please slow down. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreters also add and also pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the republican level of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that requires a broader explanation. Based on the method for the Territorial Defence of Mostar employed for it, we expect that that was the model which was applied to the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We in the Territorial Defence had a command that was of Croat and Serbian and Bosniak composition, and at the moment the reservists arrived, and perhaps even before that, I'm not quite certain at this point, the General Staff of the Yugoslav army simply excluded from the Territorial Defence and its command all non-Serb staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we perhaps now see in e-court document 5D 01094. If we do not manage to see it in e-court, then again we can see it physically. We can see it this time either -- please, can we see it physically. And I apologise for this type of technical functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: This, Mr. Gagro, is a quite short excerpt from the book by General Stjepan Siber. Tell me, he is a general of the army of B and H?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page. Of course this is the first, the cover page of the book, and on the next page the highlighted section describes the ethnic composition of the republican staff of the Territorial Defence, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And it notes that this was the way it was. Would you please read it out.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "50 per cent of Serbs -- 60 per cent of Serbs, 30 per cent of Muslims, and around 10 per cent of Croats."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Personal staff and financial departments with 100 per cent Serbians, there could be no talk about a national parity or the equality of the representation of the peoples."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: What does it say about the structure of the Territorial Defence of the republican level?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it confirms what I said about Mostar and its set-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, on page 48 of the transcript, you referred to the fact that analogously to what in your view was the HVO, actually the Muslims follow suit in their action, the Bosniaks, and you say that they too had some sort of a temporary interim government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm sorry, I didn't quite catch your drift. What government are you referring to and in what period?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: In mid-1992.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the expulsion of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Did the Muslim side on the east bank, on the east side of Mostar which was still functioning as a unified undivided city because there were no conflicts between the Croats and the Muslims as yet, did the Muslim party form any special separate bodies?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to clarify. As the Croatian Defence Council had already well advanced in its organisation, the -- we pushed the Bosniak side to actually expedite its own organisation. We didn't insist to have individuals directly engaged in HVO forces. We asked them to define their army -- military structure organisationally and that it should be within the HVO. And while the HDZ was still functioning, they managed to -- to set up a battalion, and that was a big thing. And perhaps an even different type of unit but, being no military expert, I cannot enter into their military structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So it was the 15th of May, 1992, that you were relieved of your duty and divested of all your powers?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and of all my burdens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the registrar please try to show us document 5D 01093. We will have to display it on the ELMO again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagro, this is a document which says the Crisis Staff of Mostar Municipality on the top; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: We don't know who signed it, but obviously the date is the 15th of May, 1992, precisely the date I referred to?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: The date on which you were relieved of your duties?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you explain, please, what does this mean, the end of this first sentence, "... and inform the Crisis Staff of the TO of actions taken" ? Does this mean that there was a separate TO Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably this formal one, this Territorial Defence that was -- and of course I'm only making an assumption because I see this document for the first time now, but the association that I have is that it was after all accepted that -- that the commander and his team, the Territorial Defence commander and team, were still formally functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I failed to comprehend. The Crisis Staff of the municipality is one thing and the Crisis Staff of the TO is another thing.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No such concept existed. Someone made use of that. I really fail to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Apart from yourself, was anyone else authorised to sign a document on behalf of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you rule out the possibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a stamp on the document. It says the Mostar -- it says Crisis Staff, Mostar 1. Is this a stamp that you used when you were at the head of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've never used this stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you rule out the possibility for this to be an organisational governmental form installed by the Bosniak Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can assume, because of the name indicated here, Arif Hadziosmanovic, and I don't know who that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yesterday and today, Mr. Gagro, we saw a document on the appointment of the Special Purpose Council which has 13 members, with Jadran Topic actually appointing the 13 members of that council, and we saw that there were five Muslims among them. You yourself said that one of them was Mr. Jaganjac who was the only one who did not come from Mostar, but you knew him. So you said so.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, we saw that -- the Defence team of Mr. Prlic actually showed you a document where the commander of the Territorial Defence of Mostar appoints his aides. That is the document of the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the registrar please show us that document. This is 1D 00495. I think we had it in electronic form and we'll be able to see in that form again now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: There, Mr. Gagro, we saw that the Special Purpose Council, that five Muslims had been appointed to that council.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is without a doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Well, if we can see that document, if we manage to have it shown ... Among these first seven people who have some commanding or leading roles, tell me, are there any non-Muslims among these first seven?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So they're all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I only have a last question for you, a concluding one. Today, to questions by the Defence team for General Praljak, by Mr. Kovacic, you were shown numerous photographs and you referred to a book called "The Urbicide of Mostar."

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Urbicide of the City of Mostar."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: "The Urbicide of the City of Mostar." Tell me, in this -- this book contains documents about the devastation of the city by the Yugoslav army and its associated forces, the Chetniks, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was this book a joint Croato-Muslim project, in cooperation?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And was this book -- is -- has it been -- does it document in an authentic fashion the extent of devastation?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no reason to either conceal or simplify that. It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And a final question: Was this book sold over the counter or could it be obtained in other ways?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions. And can we tender the documents shown to the witness under numbers 5D 01091, 01092, 01093.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. 01094. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. President. Those exhibits will therefore be tendered and admitted under the following references: 5D 01091, 5D 0092 [sic], 5D 00 -- sorry, 01093, and 5D 01094. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. One correction. When listing the documents, a number was omitted. The second exhibit should be 01092. The number 1 was omitted. It's page 72, line 19. And in line 20 we have an additional number: It should be 5D 01094. Number 6 has been added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I just have a few questions I'd like to clarify certain matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Mr. Jonjic has already addressed this matter but, Mr. Gagro, a minute ago you saw an order shown to you by Mr. Coric's Defence team. It's an order from General Perisic. He ordered that civilian targets in Mostar should be shelled; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's not only that he wrote this for his units. He also contacted us over the phone and said, "You'll now be put underground."

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague mentioned the date 19th of April, 1992, and you then said that there were so many of them that I couldn't remember them all. So my impression was that shelling was very frequent or done on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost on a daily basis, so we were happy when we could fall asleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: After the JNA or the Yugoslav army - call it as you will - was driven out of Mostar, from the direction of Podvelezje was Mostar shelled in 1992 and was this continued in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it wasn't shelled as intensively as when there was fighting in Mostar itself. They tried to take the town by surprise to maximise the consequences of their shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagro, did you witness the fact that General Perisic ordered that Mostar and other towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina should be bombed by the air force?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A helicopter squad was sent in to launch missiles at the Franciscan church in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that Yugoslav planes bombed Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they used planes to bomb Mostar. I think that they would use artillery more frequently. Land -- land-based weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Just one correction to the transcript. Page 73, line 20. It hasn't been recorded that the bombing of Mostar was also carried out -- or the shelling of Mostar was also carried out from the direction of Podvelezje. With regard to the shelling or bombing, on such occasions were buildings in Mostar destroyed? I'm referring to JNA bombing and shelling.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we have seen photographs, but it was difficult for us to talk about this. I didn't want to pre-judge anything, but it's true that the damage was extensive as a result of the army shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of such shelling were there human casualties on both sides of the river?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in the course of your testimony you mentioned a place called Uburak. Do you know where that is?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Is it in the vicinity of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's in the immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be true to say that after the JNA was driven out of Mostar a mass grave of Bosniaks and Croats was found?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Those people who, unfortunately, when the Serbian forces and JNA launched an attack on Mostar, those people weren't able to cross over, to flee to the western bank.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, an honest citizen in Mostar thought that there should be mutual respect between citizens in Mostar. That's the attitude they had. Unfortunately, it was a mistake to trust those who had come to occupy us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When this mass grave was exhumed, it was established those people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To follow up on the questions put to you, you said that General Perisic phoned you and said that you would be destroyed. Did you answer the phone call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. But he didn't say that we would be destroyed. He said that we would be placed underground. That means that if you want to survive, then you should dig in deep into the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he carried out the shelling after the phone call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the document that was presented a minute ago regarding the order on shelling, it says that they were going to shell locations where there were fundamentalist paramilitary forces. When you spoke to him on the phone, is that what he told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But he called me an Ustasha, and that said everything about the way in which he perceived us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In the document that Mr. Jonjic has shown us, since the lawyers are not soldiers, one thing was omitted. I'd like to ask the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One minute, Mr. Praljak. You said that the lawyers are not soldiers, but I assume that perhaps they were soldiers before they came lawyers. Do continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: General Perisic says that there would be three artillery hits on Mostar. The first shelling would last for 70 minutes, the second shelling 120 minutes, the third one 40 minutes, a total of 230 minutes. Could you show that document so that we can see this that just concerns that day, and I would like to thank the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We'll place the document on the ELMO. Yes. Have a look at the document. Mr. Praljak, put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, under item 3, can you see what it says about the shelling of Mostar? And "VU" means an artillery attack. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it 70 minutes on the first occasion, 120 minutes on the second occasion, and 40 minutes on the third occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Gagro. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All Defence teams have taken the floor. Ms. Nozica, I believe you haven't said anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the sake of the transcript, Your Honours, I would like to say thank you, but we have no questions for Mr. Gagro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: An omission on my part, Your Honour. I had made reference to a document, and I made reference to it as 3D 00275. That was the decision on the proclamation of an immediate threat of war, and perhaps we should give it a Defence number, 1D 00498. I'm told that's the correct procedure. So I'm following my orders from my co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. This document will therefore be tendered and admitted under two different Defence numbers, and this particular one will therefore be assigned the reference 1D 00498. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Before I do that, I would like to, before it's forgotten again, to tender the exhibits from the direct examination. I was again hoping to save time at the end of the day, but -- on Monday, but let me please tender those exhibits. Exhibit P 00071, P 00135, P 00157, P 00190, P 00199, P 00209, P 00219, and P 00221, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would object just one of those evidence. This is P 00157. [Interpretation] I can back this up with arguments. This is the article from the Croatian newspaper Vjesnik. This document has very little probative value, if any, because according to the title of the article, this article was drafted on the basis of a telephone conversation that the journalist had with Boban in Mostar. The journalist was in Zagreb and Boban was in Mostar. Some witnesses have already said that the telephone lines were practically down, and when the telephone lines functioned, the quality was so bad that one wonders whether one can really speak about communication or not. If you can't hear the question well and if you can't hear part of the answer well, I don't think we can talk about communication in such cases. I would say that this document has practically no probative value at all, and I see no reason for admitting this document into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Before I hear what Mr. Scott has to say, I note that we have the article that was published. It was on Saturday, the 8th -- the 11th of April, 1992, that the article was published, and it -- the transcript of a telephone conversation between a journalist and Mr. Mate Boban. So that's what we know. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the trial to date the Defence have put in a number of newspaper articles. The witness commented on this article and about Mr. Boban's characterisation of what had happened with the Crisis Staff. What Mr. Kovacic says I must say is very creative, but there's no evidence whatsoever that on the day that Mr. Boban was interviewed that there was not a crystal clear line of communication between Mr. Boban and the -- and the reporter, and to say otherwise is pure speculation. I think the document does have probative value, the witness commented on it, and we stand by our offer of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges, who have discussed the matter among themselves, believe that the Defence counsel hasn't proved that there were communication difficulties when the journalist spoke to Boban, and as a result we admit this document into evidence. Admitting a document into evidence doesn't mean that when it comes to the Judges' deliberations the document will be given probative value. This document will be considered together with other documents, other exhibits, and this doesn't mean that the Defence can't use other witnesses or other documents to show that the contents of this article are false. We have all the numbers are listed. Mr. Registrar, perform your duties, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... tendered and admitted with today's date. These are: P 00071, P 00135, P 00157, P 00190, P 00199, P 00209, P 00219, and P 00221. This completes the list. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have -- I do have, in light of the questions that have been raised in cross, a number of questions for redirect that I am sure that I cannot finish in the next seven minutes. I would ask to be able to put these questions and prepare some additional documents and present the questions at 4.00, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You haven't understood what I said this morning. This morning I said that we could finish this morning. We could continue working until 1.45 p.m. As a result, there would be no hearing from 4.00 p.m. to 7.00 p.m. So we could have our break now, resume after the break and continue working until 1.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, we'll have our break now. It's 12.20. We will have a 20-minute break, and we will resume at 12.40, and we will have one more hour at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gagro. Just a few questions following from questions from Defence counsel. Sir, just to be clear, then, as I understand your evidence as to most of the locations that were shown to you by Mr. Kovacic this morning, you cannot be sure when the particular destruction or damage shown in those photographs occurred, actually occurred; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's correct that you cannot know -- sorry, the nature of the question and answer, sir, I'm going to have to ask for some clarification. You do not know the actual dates or times of the destruction or damage shown; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, some of the various -- some of the buildings, locations and structures, they were in and around the city of Mostar. Were they hit or damaged on more than one occasion during the period between 1991 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A number of times. But if you insist upon a detail related to destruction and damage, I have to mention that when it comes to the destruction of the bridges, when they were destroyed this had repercussions on the surrounding buildings; it affected the surrounding buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course. And there are no -- I do not believe there's any dispute about the bridges, if that assists everyone. So the photographs that were shown to you today, if these photographs had been taken, say, in 1994 or 1995, or any time thereafter, these photographs would show the cumulative damage or destruction to these buildings and locations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, on whether you were the mayor of Mostar, you said at page 23 of the transcript this morning, line 3, when these questions were being put to you by Mr. Karnavas, he was asking you about the head of the Municipal Board, and at that citation you said this man, however, "wasn't given those competencies," but this part of your answer was not followed up or explained. When you said that the head of the Municipal Board was not given the competencies of the mayor, can you please explain that further.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Municipal Board is not the correct term. The President of the Executive Board. The concept of Executive Board, that is something that could reflect the tasks of the board.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, we can go back, if need be. Perhaps we can go back to page 23 of today's transcript. I may have misspoken. You said -- I believe it does refer to -- let me make sure. Sorry. Let me find my reference. Yes. The reference to Executive Board. You said in your testimony this morning when put -- questions were put to you about the head of the Executive Board, and then your answer to that question was: "He -" this person - "wasn't given those competencies." So I ask you again, can you please explain in what way the head of the Executive Board was not given those competencies.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the sense of defining any decisions unless they were verified by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you this way: I don't know the word in your language for mayor that might have been used, but when people during this time, 1991, 1992, addressed you using your official title, how did they address you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: President of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was there any other person or position in the structure of the governing authorities of Mostar municipality who would be considered the mayor if not the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our statute, there was no alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you were the head or chief of the Mostar Crisis Staff from the time of its creation until it was ordered disbanded on the 15th of May, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you the senior or top official, sir, of the Crisis Staff from the time of its formation until 15 May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Judges when the JNA or -- and/or the Montenegrin forces arrived in the Mostar area on the 19th of September, 1991, what did they do?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing they did was to enter and deploy - I've already said that - partially around the airport, partially around the Heliodrom, and partially around the North Camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when did they enter into and occupy more of the - excuse me - the city of Mostar proper and the centre of town, if they did?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't straight away. It was a long time afterwards. It was a checkmate position that we lived in. We lived in their presence, alongside their presence, without any serious difficulties for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How long did that continue?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: For about a month and a half to two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you said in your testimony today at page 43, line 20, and in fact you were proud that "for such a long time I managed us -- I managed to avoid this conflict." For how long did you manage to avoid the conflict, or to put it differently, when did the large-scale conflict or the fighting with the JNA forces begin?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the 15th of February, or possibly the beginning of March even. But for the most part, this coincided with the beginning of an all-out war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that was the 7th of April. I think that could have been there. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you're going to have to keep your voice up. Again you're speaking very, very softly, and one can hardly hear you. The 7th of April. So is it correct, sir, that you have not intended today to give the Judges the impression that there was continuous fighting between the 19th of September, 1991, and the 7th of April, 1992, have you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That was not my intention at all, because that's just not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the questions that were put to you about when various steps began to be taken to further organise things, to further organise the Crisis Staff, to further take certain steps, this in fact involved a much shorter window of time, didn't it, starting around -- only around the 7th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Our greatest problem was that they began to expand their area of occupation. They passed through town. There was provocation. Then they acted in such a way as to display their force and might and everything that goes with that display of might and force. But we didn't let ourselves be provoked, and we didn't enter into direct clashes with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Until when, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably the date that we mentioned, the 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Judges when the new Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established. Not the Territorial Defence or TO which existed under the JNA structure, but please tell the Judges when the Territorial Defence of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina was first established.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall that there had been something called the Territorial Defence under the JNA structure? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And once Bosnia and Herzegovina became an independent state and was recognised, when did Bosnia and Herzegovina establish a Territorial Defence distinct from the old JNA Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was changed at all. I assume that it was, according to the principle of each republic, creating its own Territorial Defence, and it did not live through a transformation of any kind. Maybe just in the commanding structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask that the witness please be shown Exhibit P 00150.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can look at that document, please, and can you tell the Chamber is that a document, a decision issued around the 8th of April, 1992, by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, establishing the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I could ask you to please have the Exhibit 1D 00495 displayed. If I can direct your attention, if you have that, sir, to the first line starting after the first list of seven names. Do you see the language where it says: "The following members of the old STO have remained"? And directing your attention to the next line after the next list of 13 names, does the document not also say: "The following members of the old OK STO Territorial Defence Staff reported to this staff." Sir, doesn't this document indicate, the document shown to you by the Defence, that these are references to the old TO, or Territorial Defence, the one that existed at the time before the TO created on the 8th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of this document, quite obviously there was just a transformation that took place in the organisational sense, in the structure and leadership of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as of April and May, 1992, the lawful government in Bosnia-Herzegovina was the government of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina with its seat in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could direct your attention, please, to Exhibit P 00209. For the registry's assistance. If you have that, sir, I'm directing your attention -- if you could please find --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- toward the end of the first paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff is being disbanded and all its --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before that, sir. Please, before that. If you look toward the end of the first paragraph on that document, if you can find the language that was pointed out to you before, it says: "Watching almost approvingly the deployment of the Serbian and Montenegrin reserve forces." Can you find that, please. Do you see that language?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found it because it's rather a poor copy to begin with, fairly illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps the Defence copy could be used. If we could put that on the ELMO, which I do agree is indeed a better copy. All right, sir, again, just to assist you, if you can direct your attention and find the language which says, I think it's towards the end of the first paragraph, but perhaps the paragraph format has changed, but language that says: "Watching almost approvingly the deployment of the Serbian and Montenegrin reserve forces." And just when you see that language --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. "Watching almost approvingly," and so on, "strategic points above the town."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, do you agree that your Municipal Assembly and your Crisis Staff was "watching almost approvingly the deployment of the Serbian and Montenegrin reserve forces"?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if my efforts not to enter into a conflict with them is seen as being approving or approvingly, then I can accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked questions earlier today about whether you supported the concept or the creation of something called a Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and before we end your testimony, I'd like to give you a further opportunity. When you say you supported such a thing, tell us about the form or nature or characteristics of a Croatian Community that you personally, not somebody else, but that you supported. What was your concept of this Croatian Community that you say you gave your support to?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to tire the Judges, I would just like to refer to a document that Mrs. Alaburic offered through the statute of the Croatian Democratic Community of Herceg-Bosna where it states quite explicitly what the programme and platform of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina is. I have nothing to add or subtract from that, but if you want to hear my opinion, then it was highlighted in one of the articles of the statute of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina which I respect and acknowledge as the bases upon which I built up my principles for approving the creation of a Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If counsel can assist us --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There it is. If counsel could assist me. I don't -- did not note down the number of that exhibit when it was referred to. Perhaps Ms. Alaburic could help me. The document she was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the statute of the Croatian Democratic Community -- union, and the number is P 00013, and the exhibit was admitted into evidence during the testimony and examination of expert witness Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm much obliged. With the assistance of the registry, please, could you display to the witness Exhibit P 00013.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, with that document in front of you can you please point out the specific language that you say illustrates or reflects your view, your view of a Croatian community that you gave your support to? And again, sir, I specifically ask you to give your personal view and not the view of anybody else. You say you gave your support to the creation of something called a Croatian community. I want you to tell the Judges very clearly the nature of such a community that you endorsed.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then, could you find me the article which speaks about the statutory provisions of the Croatian Democratic Community, the people in charge of the screen and the exhibits and e-court, please, with their assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'll have to go through the articles, then, one by one. Can we scroll down the articles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Down some more, please. Here we are. 10.1, article 10.1. Can we stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. For the record so there's no dispute about that, the article 10 -- section 10.1 says: "Ensuring the right to the Croatian people to self-determination including the right to succeed and achieving the statehood and sovereignty of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Is that the language you're referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, my final question to you, sir, is: You also said this morning - or perhaps it was this afternoon - that there was a plebiscite. You said there was a plebiscite, at page 56, line 22. You said there was a plebiscite to vote for and approve the creation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Could you tell the Judges when that plebiscite was held and who organised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't recall that being in the record. Perhaps we could have a page and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Page 56, line 22, please. And if I could have the assistance ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you read out what the record says, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I will.
