Question starting at line 21: "Would you also agree with me when I put it to you that the idea of Herceg-Bosna was supported by plebiscite by all Croats living in the areas of the municipalities that are associated into Herceg-Bosna." And your answer, at line 24, was, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my colleague Mr. Scott for reading out that question, because there was an error in the translation. I didn't ask about the support that was demonstrated through a plebiscite. My words were plebiscitary support to the Croat populations. Plebiscitary support. There plebiscitary is an adjective meaning unanimous, without any opposition, whole-heartedly, by acclamation, or whatever other synonyms you like to choose. So it wasn't actually a plebiscite that was implemented, it was unanimous support to the idea of Herceg-Bosna by almost all the Croats living in the area of the municipalities that were unified into Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the programme which related to culture, cultural organisation, historical organisation, and so on. That's what the decision to establish it stated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I appreciate very much the clarification by counsel which indeed is a bit of a different answer than what would have otherwise been in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: However, I still put my question to you because it's still been represented that there was some sort of virtually universal expression of support. So I'm just going to ask you, sir: Apart from what was said in the transcript, was there ever any sort of a plebiscite or referendum in which the people living in the territory claimed by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna could express their support and endorsement of that concept and that entity in the same way that there was indeed a referendum for the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Was there any such plebiscite or referendum; and if so, tell me when it was.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a few questions, unless you have a few of your own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just if it has to do with what was just said during the re-examination, because redirect focuses on that. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree. I agree, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First I'm going to go down the list. You're referred to as the top official of the Crisis Staff. Again, doesn't that mean that you only have one vote, just like everybody else, first among equals, nothing more nothing less? Is that yes?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Secondly, just -- again, I -- and I apologise for having to go over this ground again: You were the president of the Assembly. That's a legislative body, not an executive body, like a mayor; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But at that time, it wasn't defined in statutory terms that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going to ask you this question, because it's something that concerns me too. With your leave, we'll place Exhibit 135 on the ELMO, or we'll have it appear on the screen. It's a meeting that wasn't held but the document was referred to. There we have it. So this is a document that you did not sign because you said you weren't familiar with this document, but let's have a look at the beginning of the document dated the 12th of March, 1992. It says that pursuant to Article 139, et cetera - I'll skip that - but apparently 20 members of the Assembly contacted you on the 11th of March. It says that for the 13th session of the Municipal Assembly -- well, it means that -- that means that there had already been 12 previous sessions. So the Municipal Assembly of which you were the president was functioning because at least 12 meetings had been held. So can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Very well. Mr. Karnavas, a minute ago you asked the following: You said there's a Municipal Assembly, and you're the president. Mr. Karnavas asked you if you could say whether there was an Executive Board, and if there was, according to Mr. Karnavas, this Executive Board also had a president, and that would be the mayor in fact. You were the mayor of the Assembly, and the Executive Board was the body that acted. Is that how things functioned or not? During the 12 previous meetings, the 12 meetings that preceded the 13th that was not held, was there an Executive Board in existence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who was the president of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to find this. He was a member of the Mostar Crisis Staff. His name was Ismet Bajric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ismet Bajric. So he was the president of the Executive Board. So was he in fact the mayor, the person who implemented the decisions taken by the Assembly of which you were the president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When was the Crisis Staff established? Apparently it was on the 29th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around the 15th of February, as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 15th of February. When the Crisis Staff had been established, the Executive Board and Mr. Bajric, whose name you have provided us with, did the Executive Board continue to function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as soon as the Crisis Staff was formed, all powers transferred to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And at that point in time did you adopt a decision that disbanded the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That was automatic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Automatic. Very well. So according to what you say, as of the 12th of February, 1992, when the Crisis Staff was established, the Executive Board no longer existed. In fact, you then had two roles. You were the president of the Assembly, but you were also the person who had to take steps, who had to act in an executive matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. When the Crisis Staff was formed, the Assembly ceased to function, in fact, and I ceased to be its president. I then became the president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we can understand what you're saying as legal experts, when the Crisis Staff was established, all the institutions that had functioned previously stopped functioning and it was the Crisis Staff that was responsible for dealing with all problems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't want to add more confusion to the situation, but I just want to go back again. The Assembly is a legislative body; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, it is the executive body, the Executive Board, that draws up the plan, and it's their departments within the Executive Board that actually do the drafting of legislation that then goes to the Assembly, and then they would go ahead and pass it or reject it, correct, or send it back for amendment?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, anybody could draft these things. No administrative body had to do this. The Assembly had the right to specify the task and say that anyone could deal with certain tasks. Experts could deal with certain tasks. The Assembly could make such decisions. It's logical for your institution to deal with such matters and to prepare such material, but we didn't have to assign tasks to anyone in particular. We could assign tasks to those whom we trusted the most, and we had to decide about this at the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Needless to say, it is the Assembly that sits on top of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to move on with some of the other points. Talking about occupation. Was mentioned, and I guess the Prosecutor stressing April, 1992, but I want you to go back in history a little bit. Isn't it a fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina was used by the JNA as a staging area from which they could attack the Republic of Croatia prior to that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I've already said in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that we're clear on this. And of course Bosnia-Herzegovina, or the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Sarajevo government didn't do -- didn't stop the JNA from using the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina to attack the Republic of Croatia, did it? I'm not saying whether it could or not. I'm just saying it did nothing. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Just like they didn't do anything, and in fact they did not even react other than say, "It's not our war," when Ravno was razed to the ground and people were slaughtered; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are various interpretations which give a different viewpoint on the way in which Mr. Izetbegovic responded. I wouldn't want to go into such analysis. I know what Mr. Izetbegovic stated, but I think that was his personal statement. There were other members of the Presidency; there were two Croats there, there was the Prime Minister who was a Croat, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- all of these factors resulted into statements and viewpoints that differed from the statements and viewpoints of Mr. Izetbegovic who was the president of the Presidency, but this statement was his personal statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, the Judges are wondering how the issue you have raised relates to the re-examination. We're trying to understand that, although we have grasped the finesse of your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Great. Great. I'm trying not to go too far off the farm, but I think I'm still on safe territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the one thing that I wanted to comment on was, you know, on the May 15th decision, or order where they -- they asked you whether you were watching almost approvingly, that phrase. Obviously it's sort of -- it's a hurtful phrase in a sense, but if I understand it - and correct me if I'm wrong - you were hoping for the best, but as time was going by the JNA was taking more and more territory, occupying more and more. It's a bit like, say, Chamberlain with Hitler. You know, appeasing, hoping that maybe Hitler won't do anything, won't take any more countries in Western Europe, and there you are, you had the JNA day after day encroaching to the point where, there it is, April. There's no more Territorial Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm wondering if there is a question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There is a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm hoping for a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There is no effective weapons in the Territorial Defence. There is nothing left. Isn't that what we're talking about, what that they put in, whether rightly or wrongly, that you waited, hoping the situation would stop, yet the JNA continued, along with the Montenegrin reservists, to take more and more territory.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I would like to express my own viewpoint with regard to that. We knew that the policies of a Greater Serbia, that the policies established to create a Greater Serbia and the idea that the border should be Karlovac and Virovitica was an idea they were trying to implement by adopting a wider programme. Since they weren't able to implement this programme, this plan, they had reserve secondary option. That was to have a border at the Neretva. That's why they first came to Mostar, in order to achieve their objectives of a Greater Serbia. They thought that if they couldn't achieve their objectives in Croatia, then they'd try to hold firm to border the Neretva. And this was demonstrated by the destruction of the bridges on the Neretva. We weren't naive. We knew what was going on, but we were aware of our weaknesses. As I have said, we were aware of the fact that we had forces that were inadequate to confront the troops and the army from Serbia who were armed to the teeth, the troops that had come from Montenegro, too. And their only idea was to establish a border at the Neretva. That was the sole objective. So what should we do since we had no weapons? They would have defeated us in two days. In our wisdom - and I believe that we were wise - in our wisdom we tried to postpone a decisive battle until we had the pre-conditions for defending our homes. And that is why we procrastinated, why we engaged in negotiations, why we held meetings. The first commander of the corps, Topica [phoen], was first there, he was then replaced because he wasn't sufficiently radical. He wouldn't talk to us. Then they sent Mr. Perisic who also came to speak to us, to discuss things with us. So we would often meet at the northern camp in the Mostar barracks commander's office. We would speak there. And the questions were why are you here? What do you want? And finally he said that he heard that there was some sort of forces on the other side. They had to defend themselves against these forces. Unfortunately, this was HOS propaganda from Ljubuski where they had demonstrated that they had some kind of force. 40 men were used to demonstrate this force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here for a second. But during this period -- during this period while the TOs -- the weapons from the TOs are being stolen or siphoned off and everyone else is asleep and it's almost midnight in Sarajevo, the HVO at least is preparing itself for what, you know, it looks like it's going to be a conflict ahead; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally. That's what we discussed. That's why we went to Zagreb, we had meetings, and why we tried to see how we could create the pre-conditions that we required to defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why did you go to Sarajevo? I assume Sarajevo was functioning at that point in time. The central bank was working. They were able to provide the pensioners with their pension funds. They were able to provide all the amenities that a state is supposed to provide to its citizens, or was it the Sarajevo, like Mostar, was more or less under siege and unable to take care of itself let alone take care of the whole country, including Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're right. They weren't in a position to deal with the problems that they had, let alone with the problems throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that if Sarajevo could have solved the problems, you would have gone to Sarajevo, not to Zagreb? But since you went to Zagreb, that was because, in your opinion, Sarajevo couldn't help you solve the problems you faced on a daily basis in the field, and that is the reason in fact for which you went to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't go to Zagreb very frequently. We only went there once a lot earlier, before matters became complicated. We discussed what was in store for us, and we discussed the solutions we might find to the problem. Perhaps there are documents to this effect, but there were 20 letters that we sent to all the representatives in Sarajevo concerning the problems we had. This was after the JNA arrived in Mostar. Mr. Stojic was there. He probably read those letters that we addressed to everyone, seeking assistance. Unfortunately, we received no such assistance, and that was a significant problems for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood this correctly, Mr. Scott had something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I did have one additional exhibit but I don't know if there are additional Judges' questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My very last question. It concerns your testimony yesterday. You referred to the HOS, and you said that General Kraljevic had been killed, that then there was some lobbying, and finally the HOS became part of the HVO. Can you confirm this? And in your opinion, when did the HOS members actually become part of the HVO? Answer the question if you can. If not, just say so.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that you understand how this worked. There wasn't a decision according to which they said we'll now move from one area to another, from one room to another. Things developed spontaneously and over a fairly lengthy period of time. So the less extreme members of the HOS moved over, crossed over more rapidly than others who stood by their positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What happened to those who were more rigid?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they ended up in -- in a blind alley as a result of the steps taken by those who were stronger than they were. So they couldn't act in the territory that they were located in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but with the leave of the Chamber, I'd first like to explain why I have taken the floor. In this part of his testimony, the witness mentioned the name of my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to that reference, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gagro, you just mentioned Mr. Stojic. You said he was there. Please tell me, what did you mean by "there"?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, he was the assistant minister of the interior in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I apologise. This term is perhaps not quite correct, but that was our altitude towards the central authorities. We called the central authorities "there." We would say that they were "there."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. And we would say that you were down there. That's quite common in Bosnia. For the sake of the transcript, can we say when Mr. Bruno Stojic had that position in the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established, the newly elected government, Bruno Stojic represented the HDZ, and he was the assistant minister of the interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I think that he was elected at the same time as the entire government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would that be correct to say that it was after the multi-party elections in 1990 and right up to 1992, April, May, 1992? Is that the period that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you have any information according to which the Ministry of the Interior, or to be more specific, Mr. Bruno Stojic, given his field of competence in that ministry, provided to the town of Mostar weapons and other materiel and equipment during the period preceding April, 1992? And you have said with regard to that period that you contacted the state organs for aid, for assistance, requesting assistance during that period. Do you know anything about this? We don't have documents about this right now because this wasn't supposed to be the subject of your testimony. I'm only interested in your information, and we will present documents through other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, according to the information I have, the police or the security services centre in Mostar had 200 automatic rifles and some additional weapons for the reserve forces. I assume that they had 700 pieces altogether and no more than that. Unfortunately, the assessment that we only had such weapons made it clear to us what we could expect. That's why we tried to avoid provoking a conflict until it was possible to engage in a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please answer this question. It's very important for me. Did you have any information according to which perhaps some of those 700 weapons were received during that period of time from the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I just have one more question I would like to put to you and it relates to a question put to you by Mr. Scott. On a number of occasions in the course of your testimony today you said that the Crisis Staff in Mostar was established on the 15th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said yes. It hasn't been included in the transcript. It's a bit difficult to hear your answers. When you were examined by Mr. Scott, you said that the war in fact started on the 7th or 8th of April. Very briefly, as I have not got much time left, why did you establish a Crisis Staff in February?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In February, we came to the conclusion --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please finish your sentence.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In February, we came to the conclusion that war was inevitable.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be brief since we don't have much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be very brief, but the question was direct and I do have to react.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gagro, when reference was made to the photographs that I showed you, and this issue was raised again a while ago, you said that the photographs taken in relation to urbicide were taken in the autumn of 1992; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that a certain group of people were involved in this project? There were Croats and Muslims and they provided archival material, there were various specialists, cameramen, directors, equipment, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree -- agree that the material compiled was compiled in an honest manner?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the material reflected the situation in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time that those documents were compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. And in your opinion, given the material that you saw after the war, given the material you are familiar with, and given the fact that you know what the situation in Mostar was during the war, would you agree that the damage inflicted to various buildings in the course of the Croat and Muslim war was damage that added to damage that had already been inflicted? It wasn't completely new damage. What had been destroyed was destroyed, but it could be destroyed even more fully.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ GAGRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When you're destroying a town, when you're razing a town to the ground, you can hit the same building ten times in one day or over a period of one month or a period of one year. One didn't proceed segment by segment when it came to destroying the town. The town was destroyed in the way that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally, Your Honours, we'll bring in the material that the witness has referred to as soon as it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, let's deal with your exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would tender Exhibit P 00150 at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. This exhibit will be therefore tendered and admitted with today's date under the reference P 00150. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I have one technical matter to raise, a legal issue. At page 87 of the transcript today, lines 4 through 7, Mr. Scott asked the witness the following question: "Sir, as of April and May, 1992, the lawful government in Bosnia-Herzegovina was the government of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina with its seat in Sarajevo; is that correct?" And the witness answered, "Correct." Your Honour, I wish to make a technical objection to the admissibility of that answer as falling outside the competence of this witness. It's a legal question which the Trial Chamber may have occasion to rule on at a later time, and though it may not be of great importance that the answer is on the record, I do want to be on the record as making the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your objection has been recorded in the transcript. Mr. Gagro, on behalf of the Judges, I would like to thank you for having come to testify at the request of the Prosecution. You have spent two days in The Hague, and I hope that the questions weren't too trying for you. I thank you for your contribution to establishing the truth, and on behalf of the Judges I wish you a safe trip home. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom, and the Victims and Witnesses Unit will then assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank you, too, and I'm glad that I have been able to assist you in determining the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, tomorrow we will be continuing with the cross-examination of the witness, and I assume he's catching his flight now. The registrar will provide the Registry with all the necessary information so that the witness can be met at the airport so that he can be taken to his hotel and so that he can appear tomorrow morning for the hearing at 9.00, or 9.00 and one minute -- or not at 9.00 and one minute but at 9.00 sharp. Everyone will have enough time. I'll try and be a little less loquacious so that everyone has sufficient time to put questions to the witness and also that Mr. Praljak has sufficient time for his questions if he wishes to put them. Thank you, and I will see everyone tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 31st day of May, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
